::: {#thm-bonferroni-fwer}
#### The Bonferroni correction controls the FWER

If all p-values of true null hypotheses are valid (@def-valid-p-value),
the [Bonferroni correction](#def-bonferroni) at level $\siglevel$ satisfies

$$\text{FWER} \le \frac{m_0}{m} \siglevel \le \siglevel,$$

whatever the dependence between the p-values.
:::

::: proof

The first line below is @def-fwer, and the second is @sol-bonferroni-fwer.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{FWER}
&= \Prf{V \ge 1}
&& \text{(definition of the FWER)}\\
&\le \frac{m_0}{m} \siglevel
&& \text{(bound from the exercise)}\\
&\le \siglevel
&& \text{($m_0 \le m$, so $m_0 / m \le 1$)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The proof uses only the union bound and the validity of each p-value,
so it needs no assumption about how the p-values depend on each other.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#exm-bonferroni-fwer}
#### FWER of the Bonferroni correction in the simulated family

In the simulated family of @exm-rejection-counts, $m_0 / m = 0.9$,
so @thm-bonferroni-fwer bounds the FWER by $0.9 \times 0.05 =$ `r 0.9 * 0.05`.
Repeating the simulation 2000 times with the Bonferroni correction:

```{r}
#| label: fwer-bonferroni
#| code-fold: false
set.seed(574)
sim_counts$bonferroni <- run_simulation(function(p) bonferroni_reject(p, 0.05))
summarize_counts(sim_counts$bonferroni)
```

The estimated FWER, `r round(summarize_counts(sim_counts$bonferroni)[["FWER"]], 3)`,
is below the bound, up to simulation error.
The Bonferroni correction loses power in exchange:
it finds `r round(100 * summarize_counts(sim_counts$bonferroni)[["power"]])`% of the 100 false null hypotheses,
against `r round(100 * summarize_counts(sim_counts$unadjusted)[["power"]])`% for unadjusted testing.
:::
